criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: NSL Article 42(2) sets a no-bail-unless threshold for national security bail applications.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: No bail shall be granted to a criminal suspect or defendant unless the judge has sufficient grounds for believing that the criminal suspect or defendant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: No bail shall be granted to a criminal suspect or defendant unless the judge has sufficient grounds for believing that the criminal suspect or defendant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 52. It will be recalled that NSL 42(2) provides as follows: “No bail shall be granted to a criminal suspect or defendant unless the judge has sufficient grounds for believing that the criminal suspect or defendant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security.”
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFA statement of the statutory text used in construing NSL Article 42(2).

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: For NSL bail, Article 42(2) introduces a threshold materially more stringent than ordinary bail under the Criminal Procedure Ordinance.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: Plainly, NSL 42(2) introduces a considerably more stringent threshold requirement.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: Plainly, NSL 42(2) introduces a considerably more stringent threshold requirement.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 53. The following features are noteworthy: (a) The subject-matter of NSL 42(2) overlaps with the subject-matter of CPO 9G(1)(b) which makes the risk of committing an offence while on bail a basis for refusing bail. NSL 42(2) focusses on the risk of the accused committing “acts endangering national security” if bail is granted. (b) However, the starting-point of the inquiry is significantly different. Under CPO 9G(1), bail may be refused if it appears to the court that there are substantial grounds for believing that the accused person would fail to surrender to custody, commit an offence while on bail or interfere with witnesses or pervert or obstruct the course of justice. If such grounds are not positively made out, bail is granted. The rule embodies the presumption in favour of bail. Under NSL 42(2), that presumption is excluded in the first instance. The starting-point is that no bail shall be granted unless the judge has sufficient grounds for believing that the accused “will not continue to commit acts endangering national security”. Plainly, NSL 42(2) introduces a considerably more stringent threshold requirement. Under the CPO, the rule is “grant bail unless there are substantial grounds to believe violation will occur”, while under NSL 42(2) it is “no bail unless there are sufficient grounds to believe violation will not occur”. This is a distinction to which we will return in examining the decision of the learned Judge. (c) The final point of distinction is that NSL 42(2) does not refer to the risk of committing an offence but to a risk that the accused will “continue” to “commit acts endangering national security” if granted bail. Two aspects call for comment. (i) First, the word “continue” must obviously not be read as implying that the accused is somehow to be treated as guilty of having committed such acts before trial. To give it such a meaning would fly in the face of NSL 5’s adherence to the presumption of innocence. “Continuing” may best be understood to involve recognising that the defendant is alleged to have committed an offence or offences involving acts endangering national security and NSL 42(2) requires assurance that he will not commit acts of such a nature if bail is granted. (ii) Secondly, the appellant contends that the word “acts” includes acts which do not constitute of any offence. It is difficult to envisage the accused committing acts endangering national security which would not amount to offences either under the NSL or under HKSAR law. [40] Indeed, it is hard to see why NSL 42(2) would, by its “sufficient grounds” requirement, necessitate refusal of bail because the judge is not satisfied that the accused will not, if given bail, perform acts which would not constitute offences. The logic of the appellant’s construction is that the acts in question may be freely performed by anyone without breaking the law whereas such acts would necessitate refusal of bail. We would therefore construe “acts endangering national security” in the context of the NSL 42(2) requirement as referring to acts of that nature capable of constituting an offence under the NSL or the laws of the HKSAR safeguarding national security.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: NSL Article 42(2) operates as a specific exception within the existing bail regime, rather than replacing the whole bail regime.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: NSL 42(2) operates in the context or matrix of the existing bail regime and draws on its rules and principles insofar as they may be relevant, while introducing a new and more stringent threshold requirement for the grant of bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: NSL 42(2) operates in the context or matrix of the existing bail regime and draws on its rules and principles insofar as they may be relevant, while introducing a new and more stringent threshold requirement for the grant of bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 54. The aforesaid characteristics of NSL 42(2) define its limits as the specific exception carved out from the bail regime which is made otherwise applicable in relation to national security offences by NSL 4, 5, 41 and 42. NSL 42(2) operates in the context or matrix of the existing bail regime and draws on its rules and principles insofar as they may be relevant, while introducing a new and more stringent threshold requirement for the grant of bail. criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFA summarised NSL Article 42(2) as a specific exception importing a stringent threshold for bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 70. The conclusions we have so far reached may be summarised as follows. (a) The legislative acts of the NPC and NPCSC leading to the promulgation of the NSL as a law of the HKSAR in accordance with the provisions of the Basic Law and the procedure therein, are not subject to constitutional review by the Court on the basis of any alleged incompatibility as between the NSL and the Basic Law or the ICCPR as applied to Hong Kong. [58] (b) NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications. [59] (c) NSL 42(2) is to be construed and applied with the guarantees of human rights and the rule of law values affirmed by NSL 4 and NSL 5, as well as with the general procedural rules made applicable by NSL 41 and NSL 42, read as a coherent whole. (d) In applying NSL 42(2) when dealing with bail applications in cases involving offences endangering national security, the judge must first decide whether he or she “has sufficient grounds for believing that the criminal suspect or defendant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security”. In doing so: (i) The judge should consider everything that appears to the court to be relevant to making that decision, including the possible imposition of appropriate bail conditions and materials which would not be admissible as evidence at the trial. It may in particular cases be helpful to have regard to factors such as those set out in CPO 9G(2) in connection with the “sufficient grounds” question. (ii) The judge should take the reference to “acts endangering national security” to mean acts of that nature capable of constituting an offence under the NSL or the laws of the HKSAR safeguarding national security. (iii) The judge should regard the NSL 42(2) “sufficient grounds” question as a matter for the court’s evaluation and judgment and not as involving the application of a burden of proof. (e) If, having taken into account all relevant material, the judge concludes that he or she does not have sufficient grounds for believing that the accused will not continue to commit acts endangering national security, bail must be refused. (f) If, on the other hand, the judge concludes that taking all relevant material into account, he or she does have such sufficient grounds, the court should proceed to consider all other matters relevant to the grant or refusal of bail, applying the presumption in favour of bail. This includes consideration of whether there are substantial grounds for believing that the accused would fail to surrender to custody, or commit an offence (not limited to national security offences) while on bail, or interfere with a witness or pervert or obstruct the course of justice. Consideration should also be given to whether conditions aimed at securing that such violations will not occur ought to be imposed. [60] G. The Judge’s decision

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFA held that Tong (No 1) erred in a crucial respect by misapprehending the nature and effect of the NSL Article 42(2) threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: that judgment unfortunately falls into error and is flawed in a crucial respect in that it misapprehends the nature and effect of the threshold requirement laid down by NSL 42(2).
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: that judgment unfortunately falls into error and is flawed in a crucial respect in that it misapprehends the nature and effect of the threshold requirement laid down by NSL 42(2).
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 72. While much of what is said in Tong (No 1) is consistent with the foregoing analysis, that judgment unfortunately falls into error and is flawed in a crucial respect in that it misapprehends the nature and effect of the threshold requirement laid down by NSL 42(2). The Court held that: “The restriction against bail being granted under art.42 is a narrow one. Although the provision is couched in a double negative form, the substantive question which a judge has to ask, when considering the question of bail of a person charged with an offence endangering national security, is whether there are grounds, or reasons, to believe that the accused person will continue to commit ‘acts endangering national security’, ie offences under the National Security Law and not just any act which may in some way be said to endanger national security.” [64]

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: Tong treated Article 42(2) as targeting the risk of offending while on bail in respect of national security offences.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: Article 42(2), in substance, targets such risk in respect of offences endangering national security.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: Article 42(2), in substance, targets such risk in respect of offences endangering national security.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 50. In respect of the third argument, Mr Dykes contends that Article 42 enables arbitrary detention since it prevents the release of a person where there are no grounds for withholding bail, ie no risk of not attending trial or committing offences on bail or interfering with witnesses or perverting the course of justice [19] . Inherent in this argument is the acceptance that it is a proper ground to withhold bail where there is a real risk of the accused person committing offences while on bail. Article 42(2), in substance, targets such risk in respect of offences endangering national security. We do not see how it can be said that withholding bail in such a situation would give rise to arbitrary detention. GROUND 2 - THE CHIEF MAGISTRATE WAS NOT “INDEPENDENT”

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: the effect of Article 42 is to emphasize the particular weight which the bail court ought to give to the “risk of re-offending” when dealing with offences under the NSL.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 14. In my judgment, the effect of Article 42 is to emphasize the particular weight which the bail court ought to give to the “risk of re-offending” when dealing with offences under the NSL. As discussed above, the rationale behind the “risk of re-offending” as a ground for objecting bail is forward-looking in that they aim at preventing the incidence of types of behaviour prohibited by the criminal law. In the context of the NSL, the court’s common law duty in protecting and preserving national security is expressly reinforced by Article 3(3).

As has been stated by Anthea Pang J in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying , I have to make a “predictive and evaluative” exercise at this stage, of all the materials before me, whether the Court has sufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of predictive/evaluative assessment terminology.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: HKSAR v Wan Siu Kin Andrew
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, absence of sufficient grounds under the NSL threshold led to refusal of bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I do not have sufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I do not have sufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 14. Having considered the submissions of Counsel, both oral and written, and all the documents attached to the written submissions, I do not have sufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI refusal; candidate only.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: HKSAR v Mo Man Ching Claudia
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI considered materials, submissions and proposed bail conditions in a predictive and evaluative NSL bail assessment, but refused bail where sufficient grounds were absent.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: after performing my “predictive and evaluative” exercise, on the materials before me, and counsel’s submissions, both written and oral, and the bail conditions offered, I consider that there are insufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: after performing my “predictive and evaluative” exercise, on the materials before me, and counsel’s submissions, both written and oral, and the bail conditions offered, I consider that there are insufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 21. I have always had the upmost respect for journalists, particularly those reporting the news impartially and reflecting the situation accurately and without bias. Having heard and seen what the Applicant had said, I am of the view that, after performing my “predictive and evaluative” exercise, on the materials before me, and counsel’s submissions, both written and oral, and the bail conditions offered, I consider that there are insufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI refusal after considering proposed conditions.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI applied Lai CFA by considering all relevant matters, including possible bail conditions and materials not admissible at trial.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: the judge should consider everything that appears to the court to be relevant to making that decision, including the possible imposition of appropriate bail conditions and materials which would not be admissible as evidence at the trial
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: the judge should consider everything that appears to the court to be relevant to making that decision, including the possible imposition of appropriate bail conditions and materials which would not be admissible as evidence at the trial
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 12. The CFA judgment also elucidated that in applying NSL 42(2), the Judge must first decide if there are sufficient grounds for believing that the suspect or defendant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security (“the prohibited acts”). In doing so, “the judge should consider everything that appears to the court to be relevant to making that decision, including the possible imposition of appropriate bail conditions and materials which would not be admissible as evidence at the trial”. [7]
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of CFA all-relevant-materials approach.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, imposed bail conditions satisfied the court that the applicant would not continue NSL offences if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: with the conditions that I have imposed for bail, that he will not continue to commit any offences under the NSL if bail is granted to him.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: with the conditions that I have imposed for bail, that he will not continue to commit any offences under the NSL if bail is granted to him.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 25. Overall, I am satisfied that with the conditions that I have imposed for bail, that he will not continue to commit any offences under the NSL if bail is granted to him.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI grant illustration; not a general rule without review.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Wong Pik Wan
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI treated Lai CFA as establishing that NSL 42(2) creates a stringent threshold exception to ordinary bail principles.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 4. The applicable principle as reiterated by the CFA judgment in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [4] at paragraph 70(b) was: “NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications.”
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of Lai CFA threshold formulation.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Wong Pik Wan
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, the CFI refused a prosecution review after finding insufficient grounds to believe the respondent would continue NSL acts if bailed.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: Having weighed all the materials before me, I am satisfied there are insufficient grounds for believing that the Respondent will continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted to her.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: Having weighed all the materials before me, I am satisfied there are insufficient grounds for believing that the Respondent will continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted to her.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 8. As was pointed out by Anthea Pang J in the case of HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [6] , it is “a predictive and evaluative exercise” that I must do, taking into account as the Court of Final Appeal pointed out, all the materials before me including submissions of counsel, documents and videos, make an evaluation as to whether under the first threshold that I can believe that the Respondent will not continue to commit acts endangering national security. Having weighed all the materials before me, I am satisfied there are insufficient grounds for believing that the Respondent will continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted to her.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive grant/continued-bail illustration following Lai CFA.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Or Yiu Lam Ricky
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, the CFI found sufficient grounds under the NSL first threshold for the respondent not to continue NSL acts if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: sufficient grounds exist for believing that the Respondent “will not continue to commit acts endangering national security” if bail is granted to him.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: sufficient grounds exist for believing that the Respondent “will not continue to commit acts endangering national security” if bail is granted to him.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 8. Having considered all the materials before me, the written and oral submissions of both counsel, I have come to the conclusion that sufficient grounds exist for believing that the Respondent “will not continue to commit acts endangering national security” if bail is granted to him. So I found that the Respondent has successfully persuaded this Court over the first threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive grant/continued-bail illustration following Lai CFA.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI considered all materials, submissions and even potentially inadmissible materials in making the predictive NSL bail evaluation.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: On all the materials which had been placed before me, including counsel’s submissions, both written and oral, including documents or materials which may not be admissible at trial, in order for me to make a predictive evaluation.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: On all the materials which had been placed before me, including counsel’s submissions, both written and oral, including documents or materials which may not be admissible at trial, in order for me to make a predictive evaluation.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 14. In order for the Applicant to overcome the first threshold, Anthea Pang J pointed out in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [13] that this Court has to make a “predictive and evaluative exercise”. On all the materials which had been placed before me, including counsel’s submissions, both written and oral, including documents or materials which may not be admissible at trial, in order for me to make a predictive evaluation.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of all-relevant-materials approach following Lai CFA.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, the CFI refused bail because sufficient grounds under the NSL first threshold were absent.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I cannot find sufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I cannot find sufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 15. I can only say that based on the materials before me, I cannot find sufficient grounds for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if granted bail. So I find that the Applicant had failed to overcome the first threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI refusal; candidate only.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI repeated that the NSL bail test requires a predictive and evaluative exercise.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: the court has to make “a predictive and evaluative exercise”.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: the court has to make “a predictive and evaluative exercise”.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 19. In determining whether the Applicant had passed the first threshold as laid down by the CFA in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying , as Anthea Pang J (as she then was) said in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [8] that the court has to make “a predictive and evaluative exercise”.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of predictive/evaluative assessment terminology.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, the CFI was not satisfied that the applicant would not continue NSL-endangering acts if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I am not satisfied that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering NSL if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I am not satisfied that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering NSL if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 20. Having heard and seen the documents and videos, and also read and heard the submissions of both counsel, I am not satisfied that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering NSL if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI refusal; candidate only.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI restated that this form of NSL bail application requires a predictive and evaluative exercise.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: the judge on a bail application of this nature has to make a “predictive and evaluative” exercise
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: the judge on a bail application of this nature has to make a “predictive and evaluative” exercise
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 21. As had always been stated previously, the judge on a bail application of this nature has to make a “predictive and evaluative” exercise as Anthea Pang J (as she then was) had said in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [6] , on all the available evidence before the court. Even matters which may turned out to be inadmissible in a trial.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of predictive/evaluative assessment terminology.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI considered the words used, circumstances, submissions and possible bail conditions in assessing future NSL risk.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: consider all of them, together with the submissions, and also the possible, conditions of bail, whether the Applicant will continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: consider all of them, together with the submissions, and also the possible, conditions of bail, whether the Applicant will continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 22. Of course, that will take into account the words actually used, the demeanor when it was said, the setting in which it was said, and also the various occasions when matters were said by the Applicant. To distill it into a pot, and consider all of them, together with the submissions, and also the possible, conditions of bail, whether the Applicant will continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of all-relevant-materials and possible-conditions approach.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: HKSAR v Fung Tat Chun Frankie
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI described the sequence for NSL bail: first the Article 42 threshold, then the ordinary Criminal Procedure Ordinance threshold only if the first is satisfied.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: it is only if the Court concludes there were sufficient grounds then the Court would then proceed to consider the application applying the second threshold, which is under the Criminal Procedure Ordinance, Cap 221, section 9N.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: it is only if the Court concludes there were sufficient grounds then the Court would then proceed to consider the application applying the second threshold, which is under the Criminal Procedure Ordinance, Cap 221, section 9N.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 8. This case is part of a series of bail applications that had come before this Court, and the principle in considering bail is derived from the Court of Final Appeal’s judgment in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying that stated that bail consideration under the NSL are considerably more stringent. The Court of Final Appeal said that the Court must first decide whether there were sufficient grounds “for believing that the accused will not continue to commit acts endangering national security”, which is the first threshold, and it is only if the Court concludes there were sufficient grounds then the Court would then proceed to consider the application applying the second threshold, which is under the Criminal Procedure Ordinance, Cap 221, section 9N.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of sequential NSL then ordinary bail thresholds.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: HKSAR v Fung Tat Chun Frankie
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, failure to overcome the first NSL threshold led to refusal of bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I am not satisfied that the Applicant had overcome the first threshold. So, the application was refused.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I am not satisfied that the Applicant had overcome the first threshold. So, the application was refused.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 29. At the end of the day, I am not satisfied that the Applicant had overcome the first threshold. So, the application was refused. criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI refusal; candidate only.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Tam Man Ho Jeremy Jansen
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI treated NSL bail assessment as a difficult predictive/evaluative exercise requiring consideration of all materials, including non-trial-admissible materials.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: It is not an easy exercise and the Court had to take into account all the materials, including materials that may not be admissible as evidence at trial, to make an evaluation as to whether the Respondent will continue to commit offences under the NSL.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: It is not an easy exercise and the Court had to take into account all the materials, including materials that may not be admissible as evidence at trial, to make an evaluation as to whether the Respondent will continue to commit offences under the NSL.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 11. As Anthea Pang J had stated in the case of HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [7] , it is “a predictive and evaluative exercise” that one had to do when considering the first threshold as stipulated by the Court of Final Appeal in dealing with bail application under the NSL. It is not an easy exercise and the Court had to take into account all the materials, including materials that may not be admissible as evidence at trial, to make an evaluation as to whether the Respondent will continue to commit offences under the NSL. There is no doubt the Respondent was key signatory of the letter to United States Congress and his influence is evidenced by many invitations to meet the United States Counsel.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of Lai CFA and post-CFA Lai CFI all-materials approach.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Tam Man Ho Jeremy Jansen
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, the CFI found no sufficient grounds under the NSL first threshold and revoked bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I am satisfied that there are no sufficient grounds for believing that the Respondent will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I am satisfied that there are no sufficient grounds for believing that the Respondent will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 12. Having considered all the materials before me, including counsels’ submissions, both written and oral, I am satisfied that there are no sufficient grounds for believing that the Respondent will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive prosecution review allowing revocation of bail.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Kwok Ka Ki
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI described its role on NSL bail review as evaluating all materials in a predictive and evaluative exercise to determine the first threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I am tasked with the function, as Anthea Pang J said, of evaluating all the materials in “a predictive and evaluative exercise”, to determine if the Respondent can pass the first threshold as laid down by the Court of Final Appeal in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I am tasked with the function, as Anthea Pang J said, of evaluating all the materials in “a predictive and evaluative exercise”, to determine if the Respondent can pass the first threshold as laid down by the Court of Final Appeal in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 12. I have no doubt that the Respondent had over the years contributed his service for good to the community at large. I also accept with great respect his record in LegCo as to his service to the community. However, I am tasked with the function, as Anthea Pang J said, of evaluating all the materials in “a predictive and evaluative exercise”, to determine if the Respondent can pass the first threshold as laid down by the Court of Final Appeal in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [12] .
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of Lai CFA first-threshold structure.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Kwok Ka Ki
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI considered all materials, submissions and existing bail conditions before revoking bail on NSL first-threshold grounds.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I have considered all the materials before me, submissions, both oral and written of counsel, and the bail conditions imposed by the learned Chief Magistrate
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I have considered all the materials before me, submissions, both oral and written of counsel, and the bail conditions imposed by the learned Chief Magistrate
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 13. In fulfilling the exercise, I do not have to consider whether the learned Chief Magistrate had made a mistake or was plainly wrong in his decision. I have considered all the materials before me, submissions, both oral and written of counsel, and the bail conditions imposed by the learned Chief Magistrate, at the end of the day, I cannot say that “sufficient grounds exist for believing that the Respondent will not continue to commit acts endangering national security” if bail is granted to him.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive prosecution review; bail conditions considered but insufficient.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI restated that NSL bail assessment requires a predictive and evaluative exercise.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I have to do a “predictive and evaluative” exercise as Anthea Pang J had indicated in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I have to do a “predictive and evaluative” exercise as Anthea Pang J had indicated in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 18. In considering whether the Applicant had passed the first threshold as laid down by the Court of Final Appeal in the case of HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying , I have to do a “predictive and evaluative” exercise as Anthea Pang J had indicated in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [12] .
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: CFI application of predictive/evaluative assessment terminology.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, the CFI considered proposed bail conditions but was not satisfied that the NSL first threshold was met.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: Having considered all the relevant materials, including the terms of bail conditions offered, I am not satisfied that sufficient grounds existed for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: Having considered all the relevant materials, including the terms of bail conditions offered, I am not satisfied that sufficient grounds existed for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 20. Having considered all the relevant materials, including the terms of bail conditions offered, I am not satisfied that sufficient grounds existed for believing that the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if granted bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI refusal after considering bail conditions.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, extra bail conditions satisfied the CFI that the respondent would not continue acts endangering national security.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: with the extra conditions I have imposed as conditions for bail, I believe that the Respondent will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: with the extra conditions I have imposed as conditions for bail, I believe that the Respondent will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 15. I have read the submissions of both counsel, the submitted documents, and also the affirmations and character references, and as was pointed out by Anthea Pang J (as she then was) in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [2] , I have to make what is called “a predictive and evaluative exercise” on the materials before me. And having considered everything that has been submitted before me, I consider that with the extra conditions I have imposed as conditions for bail, I believe that the Respondent will not continue to commit acts endangering national security if bail is granted.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI grant illustration; candidate only.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: On the facts, the CFI refused bail because the applicant failed to overcome the NSL first threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: I am not satisfied that if bail is granted, the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security. So, he had failed to overcome the first threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: I am not satisfied that if bail is granted, the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security. So, he had failed to overcome the first threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 19. Having read the documents supplied by both the Applicant and the Respondent, I have come to the conclusion, therefore, that I am not satisfied that if bail is granted, the Applicant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security. So, he had failed to overcome the first threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.lineage_note: Fact-sensitive CFI refusal; candidate only.

criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: it is now settled that the offence is subject to NSL Article 42(2) in consideration of bail.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: it is now settled that the offence is subject to NSL Article 42(2) in consideration of bail.

Finally, I will point out here that as for the additional count of “conspiracy print, publish, sell, offer for sale, distribute, display and/or produce seditious publications”, contrary to section 10(1)(c), and sections 159A and 159C of the Crimes Ordinance, Cap 200, as Mr Chau submitted, it is now settled that the offence is subject to NSL Article 42(2) in consideration of bail. criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.case_name: HKSAR v Ng Man Yee Carol
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.proposition_text: The CFI applied Lai CFA as establishing the stringent NSL Article 42(2) bail threshold.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.supporting_quote: NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.exact_quote: NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications.
criminal_procedure_hk.nsl_bail.paragraph_text: 4. The applicable principle as reiterated by the CFA judgment in HKSAR v Lai Chee Ying [4] at paragraph 70(b) was: “NSL 42(2) creates a specific exception to the HKSAR rules and principles governing the grant and refusal of bail, and imports a stringent threshold requirement for bail applications.”

criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.proposition_text: When assessing NSL Article 42(2), the court may consider whether bail conditions affect the future risk assessment.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.supporting_quote: it makes no sense presumptively to exclude bail conditions from consideration.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.exact_quote: it makes no sense presumptively to exclude bail conditions from consideration.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.paragraph_text: 57. We do not accept that argument. In the first place, it fails adequately to take account of the nature of bail itself. A person who is admitted to bail, as CPO 9C states, is released by the court from detention “on his undertaking that he shall surrender to custody on the day that the court may appoint”. All bail decisions therefore involve a risk assessment looking to the future: Can the accused’s undertaking to surrender to custody be accepted? Will he offend while on bail? Will he interfere with witnesses or the course of justice? It makes no sense to confine the court to looking only at the evidence available at the time of the bail hearing and to exclude consideration of matters which may have a bearing on the accused’s likely conduct pending the trial. Such matters include the potentially preventive effect of appropriate bail conditions which might be put in place. Of course in any given case, the judge, in answering the NSL 42(2) question, may decide that in all the circumstances, and having duly considered possible bail conditions, he or she does not have sufficient grounds for believing that the defendant will not continue to commit acts endangering national security and thus refuse bail. But it makes no sense presumptively to exclude bail conditions from consideration.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.lineage_note: CFA rejects a sealed-off first stage that excludes proposed bail conditions.

criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.proposition_text: Appropriate bail conditions may be relevant to the risk assessment because they can deter breach or further offending.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.supporting_quote: The imposition of appropriate conditions therefore possesses a deterrent value that may plainly be relevant to the risk assessment.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.exact_quote: The imposition of appropriate conditions therefore possesses a deterrent value that may plainly be relevant to the risk assessment.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.paragraph_text: 58. Secondly, the applicability of the general bail regime mandated by NSL 4, 5, 41 and 42, subject to the specific exception introduced by NSL 42(2), supports taking account of bail conditions. Thus, CPO 9D(2) provides for the imposition of bail conditions “to secure” that the person admitted to bail will duly surrender to custody and will not commit violations during the period of bail. There is in principle, no reason why the judge, in asking whether he or she has “sufficient grounds”, should not have regard to CPO 9D(2) and factor in any possible bail conditions aimed at securing that the accused will not commit acts endangering national security if granted bail. The defendant will be aware that bail will immediately be revoked if any bail condition is breached. The imposition of appropriate conditions therefore possesses a deterrent value that may plainly be relevant to the risk assessment.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.lineage_note: CFA connects conditions to risk management and deterrence.

criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.proposition_text: In NSL bail review, the court's future-risk assessment is a judgment on what the accused may or may not do in the future.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.supporting_quote: The judge has to form a view on what the accused person may or may not do in the future.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.exact_quote: The judge has to form a view on what the accused person may or may not do in the future.
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.paragraph_text: 17. As regards the matters concerning the onus or standard of proof, I have already mentioned that the strict rules of evidence are inappropriate in the court’s making of a determination on bail. In the same vein, the court said in the Habeas Corpus Judgment [22] that: “[i]t is not helpful to approach this question by reference to considerations such as the burden, or standard, of proof … The judge has to form a view on what the accused person may or may not do in the future. This is not something which is susceptible to exact proof as a matter of fact, but is a matter of judgment which the judge has to make upon an overall assessment of the relevant materials and circumstances before the court.” Reference was made to the approach there to analogous questions adopted by Lord Bingham of Cornhill in R v Lichniak [23] , by Lord Steyn in R (McCann) v Crown Court at Manchester [24] , and by Lord Carswell in R (O) v Crown Court at Harrow [25] .
criminal_procedure_hk.bail_factors.lineage_note: Useful candidate paragraph on the predictive nature of bail risk assessment.

Section 9(1) of the CO provides that: “(1) A seditious intention is an intention – (a) to bring into hatred or contempt or to excite disaffection against [the Central People’s Government], [70] or against [the Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (“HKSAR”)]; or (b) to excite [the inhabitants of the HKSAR] to attempt to procure the alteration, otherwise than by lawful means, of any other matter in [the HKSAR] as by law established; or (c) to bring into hatred or contempt or to excite disaffection against the administration of justice in [the HKSAR]; or (d) to raise discontent or disaffection amongst [the inhabitants of the HKSAR]; (e) to promote feelings of ill-will and enmity between different classes of [the population of the HKSAR]; or (f) to incite persons to violence; or (g) to counsel disobedience to law or to any lawful order.” Section 9(2) then stipulates four sets of circumstances in which an act, speech or publication is not seditious: “(2) An act, speech or publication is not seditious by reason only that it intends— (a) to show that [the Central People’s Government, or the Government of the HKSAR] has been misled or mistaken in any of [their measures]; or (b) to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of [the HKSAR] as by law established or in legislation or in the administration of justice with a view to the remedying of such errors or defects; or (c) to persuade [the inhabitants of the HKSAR] to attempt to procure by lawful means the alteration of any matter in [the HKSAR] as by law established; or (d) to point out, with a view to their removal, any matters which are producing or have a tendency to produce feelings of ill-will and enmity between different classes of [the population of the HKSAR].”

criminal_law_hk.sedition.section10_offen.paragraph_text: 48. Section 10 goes on to provide: “(1) Any person who – (a) does or attempts to do, or makes any preparation to do, or conspires with any person to do, any act with a seditious intention; or (b) utters any seditious words; or (c) prints, publishes, sells, offers for sale, distributes, displays or reproduces any seditious publication; or (d) imports any seditious publication, unless he has no reason to believe that it is seditious, shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable for a first offence to a fine at level 2 and to imprisonment for 2 years and for a subsequent offence to imprisonment for 3 years …” And “seditious word” means words having a seditious intention: section 10(5). For present purposes, offences provided for under section 10 are referred as “section 10 offences” and an offence under section 10(1)(b), with which we are concerned in the present proceedings, “a section 10(1)(b) offence”.

criminal_law_hk.sedition.procedure_juris.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal treated the Secretary for Justice written-consent requirement as a procedural safeguard for sedition prosecutions.
criminal_law_hk.sedition.procedure_juris.supporting_quote: no prosecution of a section 10 offence shall be instituted without the written consent of the Secretary for Justice
criminal_law_hk.sedition.procedure_juris.exact_quote: no prosecution of a section 10 offence shall be instituted without the written consent of the Secretary for Justice
criminal_law_hk.sedition.procedure_juris.paragraph_text: 141. Further, under section 11(2) of the CO, no prosecution of a section 10 offence shall be instituted without the written consent of the Secretary for Justice. Such procedural safeguard serves two purposes. First, it avoids the risks of law enforcement agents using subjective moral or value judgment as the basis for enforcement. Second, in line with longstanding international practice under the common law, part 5 of the Prosecution Code stipulates that a decision to prosecute has to satisfy two conditions. The first is that the admissible evidence available is sufficient to justly instituting or continuing proceedings. The second is that the general public interest must require that the prosecution be conducted. Further, according to the Prosecution Code, at §6.1, consent to prosecute is a safeguard to ensure that an appropriate level of scrutiny is exercised in cases where it is required. As such, it ensures that the right to free expression said to be engaged in a given case is properly evaluated by the Secretary for Justice in terms of sufficiency of evidence or general public interest, as the case may be, before the prosecution of a section 10 offence is allowed to be brought.

More importantly, as seen, [100] the delineation in section 9 between what is seditious and what is not does not inhibit or have the effect of inhibiting open and frank dialogue and full and vigorous debate to promote societal development and the resolution of conflicts, tensions and problems. criminal_law_hk.sedition.meaning_context.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal described the meaning of alleged seditious words as an objective contextual assessment by the court as a reasonable person.
criminal_law_hk.sedition.meaning_context.supporting_quote: It is a question of fact, entailing an objective assessment by the court as a reasonable person to ascertain the meaning of the words in the context in which they were uttered
criminal_law_hk.sedition.meaning_context.exact_quote: It is a question of fact, entailing an objective assessment by the court as a reasonable person to ascertain the meaning of the words in the context in which they were uttered
criminal_law_hk.sedition.meaning_context.paragraph_text: 149. What section 9(1) asks is whether the words uttered express a seditious intention as defined. It is a question of fact, entailing an objective assessment by the court as a reasonable person to ascertain the meaning of the words in the context in which they were uttered. Generally speaking, the context includes the state of society; the state of public feeling or sentiment; the audience addressed; the occasion, the venue, and the means of the utterance: see R v Burns & Ors (1886) 16 Cox 355; R v Aldred (1909) 22 Cox 1; Boucher , at p.281.

criminal_law_hk.sedition.meaning_context.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal held that audience understanding depends on context; ordinary public language is assessed by the court using its own reasonable-person judgment.
criminal_law_hk.sedition.meaning_context.supporting_quote: The relevance of the audience’s understanding of the meaning of the words depends on the specific context
criminal_law_hk.sedition.meaning_context.exact_quote: The relevance of the audience’s understanding of the meaning of the words depends on the specific context
criminal_law_hk.sedition.meaning_context.paragraph_text: 150. The relevance of the audience’s understanding of the meaning of the words depends on the specific context. For example, where the words are argots or coded language peculiar to the audience, their understanding of the meaning of the words will be relevant. The court as a reasonable person in that situation needs to have regard to their understanding in order to ascertain if the words carried any seditious intention. Barring such incidents, where for example the words are ordinary language uttered to the public at large, the court will exercise its own judgment as a reasonable person to ascertain their meaning.

[6] It follows that unless expressly or impliedly excluded by statute, the doctrine of joint enterprise, including its coverage of perpetrators not present at the scene, applies to unlawful assembly and riot under sections 18 and 19 of the Public Order Ordinance, Cap 245 (“POO”).

criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Tong Wai Hung and Others
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal described the fundamental principle that a secondary party is guilty of the same offence as the principal.
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.supporting_quote: it is a fundamental principle of the criminal law that a secondary party is guilty of the same offence as the principal
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.exact_quote: it is a fundamental principle of the criminal law that a secondary party is guilty of the same offence as the principal
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.paragraph_text: 29. First, it is a fundamental principle of the criminal law that a secondary party is guilty of the same offence as the principal: R v Jogee , [2017] AC 387, at [1]. While the UK Supreme Court’s remark is directed at accessories, the same must be true for parties liable under the doctrine of joint enterprise. That is because for such parties, each of them is criminally liable for all the acts done in furtherance of the joint enterprise : Sze Kwan Lung , supra, at [34].

criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Tong Wai Hung and Others
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal distinguished derivative accessorial liability from independent joint-enterprise liability.
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.supporting_quote: while an accessory’s liability is derivative, a party to a joint enterprise attracts independent liability
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.exact_quote: while an accessory’s liability is derivative, a party to a joint enterprise attracts independent liability
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.paragraph_text: 30. Second, while an accessory’s liability is derivative, a party to a joint enterprise attracts independent liability. Under the accessorial rules, only if it is proved that the principal offence has been committed (even if the identity of the principal is not known) can an alleged accessory’s liability be established. Otherwise the defendant may be guilty of an inchoate offence of conspiracy, incitement or attempt but not as an accessory. See Chan Kam Shing , supra, at [14]. On the other hand, the doctrine of joint enterprise is a common law tool developed by the courts to overcome evidential and situational uncertainties encountered in the application of the traditional accessorial rules (see Chan Kam Shing , at [15]-[31]). It is a distinct doctrine from the traditional accessory rules, although there are situations where those rules may overlap. And liability is not derivative. It is not dependent on proving that the principal committed the main offence and that the secondary party assisted or encouraged its commission. Liability is independently based on each defendant’s participation in a joint criminal enterprise with the requisite mental state to constitute the offence relevant to the defendant in question. See Chan Kam Shing , supra, at [33].

criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Tong Wai Hung and Others
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal identified two interpretative factors: common-law principles were intended to be retained unless displaced, and overcharging should be avoided.
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.supporting_quote: Those common law principles should continue to apply unless on a proper construction they do not
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.exact_quote: Those common law principles should continue to apply unless on a proper construction they do not
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.paragraph_text: 44. Two interpretative factors arise from the legislative history that help inform the construction of sections 18 and 19: (1) Unlawful assembly and riot were previously common law offences. The basic common law principles pertaining to them were meant to be retained when sections 18 and 19 were introduced. Those common law principles should continue to apply unless on a proper construction they do not. (2) The amendments to sections 18 and 19 in 1970 were introduced to address the risk of overcharging otherwise innocent persons caught up in an unlawful assembly or riot. Thus overcharging should be avoided in construing the two sections. F2. Public interest considerations

criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Tong Wai Hung and Others
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal distinguished provisions defining principal-offender liability from rules governing accessories and parties to joint enterprise.
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.supporting_quote: They do not concern the liability of accessories or parties to a joint enterprise including those who are not present at the scene
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.exact_quote: They do not concern the liability of accessories or parties to a joint enterprise including those who are not present at the scene
criminal_law_hk.public_order.joint_enter.paragraph_text: 66. A more fundamental fallacy in Mr Pun’s argument is this. Sections 18 and 19 are the primary offence-creating provisions. They define the offences and set out their ingredients plainly with principal offenders in mind. The dual requirements that this Court approved in Leung Tin Kei , supra, deal with the liability of principal offenders at the scene. They do not concern the liability of accessories or parties to a joint enterprise including those who are not present at the scene. As rightly submitted by Mr Kwok, the principles that this Court propounded in Leung Tin Kei , supra, do not displace the ordinary common law principle relating to accessories or parties to a joint enterprise, including those who are not at the scene. Put differently, the liability of the principal offenders of unlawful assembly or riot is determined under sections 18 and 19 as defined and interpreted by the courts in the case law; whereas the liability of accessories or parties to a joint enterprise is determined by reference to the accessorial rules or the doctrine of joint enterprise, as the case may be. Conflating the two, as Mr Pun seemed to have done, cannot be right.

criminal_law_hk.public_order.presence_sc.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Tong Wai Hung and Others
criminal_law_hk.public_order.presence_sc.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal stated that mere presence as a peaceful demonstrator, bystander, or onlooker without more will not render a person liable.
criminal_law_hk.public_order.presence_sc.supporting_quote: his mere presence without more will not render him liable under section 18 or 19
criminal_law_hk.public_order.presence_sc.exact_quote: his mere presence without more will not render him liable under section 18 or 19
criminal_law_hk.public_order.presence_sc.paragraph_text: 80. When a peaceful demonstration degenerates into unlawful assembly or even riot, common sense dictates that a peaceful demonstrator or a by-stander or onlooker should leave the scene as soon as reasonably practicable. If he does not do so for some good reason, or cannot because of the actual circumstances at the scene, his mere presence without more will not render him liable under section 18 or 19. However, if he becomes involved in the violence or the threat of violence or, using the language of sections 18 and 19 of the POO, a breach of peace, he crosses the line separating legally protected peaceful assembly and demonstration from unlawful activity, which is subject to legal sanctions and constraints: Chow Nok Hang, ibid. He ceases to be a peaceful demonstrator or by-stander or onlooker and should be held liable for his crime. Depending on the actual circumstances and evidence, he may be involved in the violence or threat of violence as (a) a principal or (b) an accessory or a party to a joint enterprise. In case (a), prosecuting him is of course not overcharging. Likewise, in case (b), prosecuting him under section 18 or 19 is not overcharging, but rather a legitimate step to hold him liable for his crime.

criminal_law_hk.public_order.rights_over.paragraph_text: 48. In our view, when considering whether the doctrine of joint enterprise has been excluded by sections 18 and 19, the court must adopt a construction which gives full recognition to these public interest considerations. On the one hand, the construction must ensure that all the perpetrators of the offences are caught by the sections so that public order is effectively maintained. We will elaborate on this consideration in Part F3 below. On the other hand, the construction should avoid the risk of over-charging where innocent persons caught up in an unlawful assembly or even riot might find themselves exposed to criminal liability, which would unduly restrict the right of lawful and peaceful assembly. This consideration accords with the second interpretative factor we distilled from the legislative history at [44] above. We will discuss it in Part F4 below. F3. Maintaining public order

criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.paragraph_text: 103. For reasons expanded upon below, we are of the view that a search of the digital contents of a mobile phone (as opposed to the mobile phone itself as an object) as a specie of the power of search by law enforcement officer incidental to arrest is governed by the common law instead of Section 50(6) [64] . Also, as explained below, we do not and need not have the doctrine of exigent circumstances under our common law in Hong Kong. With the familiarity by those responsible for administration of criminal justice in Hong Kong with the concept of reasonable practicality as the guide for search without warrant, we are of the view that this should also be a guide for warrantless search of the digital contents of mobile phone under our common law when such power is exercised by a law enforcement officer.

criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.case_name: Sham Wing Kan v Commissioner of Police
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal held that any warrantless search of digital phone contents must satisfy the proportionality test.
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.supporting_quote: any warrantless search must be subject to scrutiny under the proportionality test
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.exact_quote: any warrantless search must be subject to scrutiny under the proportionality test
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.paragraph_text: 106. As held in Keen Lloyd , any warrantless search must be subject to scrutiny under the proportionality test. The set of criteria permitting a warrantless search of digital contents of a mobile phone must serve legitimate interests, rationally connected with such interests and the permitted search should be no more than necessary to accomplish such interests. In the context of the protection of privacy interest when an individual is subject to warrantless search, the courts will be vigilant in ensuring that adequate and effective safeguards against abuse are in place with strict limits on such power of search [65] .

criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.case_name: Sham Wing Kan v Commissioner of Police
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal applied Keen Lloyd safeguards, emphasizing prior judicial scrutiny for intrusive warrantless digital searches.
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.supporting_quote: the general considerations discussed therein on the importance of safeguards by way of prior judicial scrutiny apply equally to a search of the digital contents of a mobile phone
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.exact_quote: the general considerations discussed therein on the importance of safeguards by way of prior judicial scrutiny apply equally to a search of the digital contents of a mobile phone
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_search_with.paragraph_text: 105. Though the Court was not concerned with the power of search incidental to arrest in Keen Lloyd , in our view the general considerations discussed therein on the importance of safeguards by way of prior judicial scrutiny apply equally to a search of the digital contents of a mobile phone even in the context of a search incidental to arrest. As will be discussed below, a warrant can be obtained under Section 50(7) for the search of the digital contents of a mobile phone. Given the engagement of the rights protected under BOR 14 and BL 30 and the potentially high privacy interest of the digital contents stored in a mobile phone (which in many cases would be even higher than the privacy interest engaged in a search of private premises), we hold that even in the context of a search of such materials incidental to an arrest a warrant should be obtained before a search unless it is not reasonably practicable to do so. In processing an application for such warrant, a judicial officer must bear in mind the judicial gatekeeping role discussed under Section B3 in the judgment of Keen Lloyd .

criminal_law_hk.fraud.case_name: HKSAR v Mo Yuk Ping and Another
criminal_law_hk.fraud.proposition_text: For section 16A fraud, concealment attracts criminal liability only if made in breach of a duty of disclosure.
criminal_law_hk.fraud.supporting_quote: a concealment attracts criminal liability only if it was made in breach of a duty of disclosure
criminal_law_hk.fraud.exact_quote: a concealment attracts criminal liability only if it was made in breach of a duty of disclosure
criminal_law_hk.fraud.paragraph_text: 3. The Court held that in relation to the actus reus of a section 16A offence, under well-established common law principles, a concealment attracts criminal liability only if it was made in breach of a duty of disclosure. To secure a conviction, the prosecution had to prove beyond reasonable doubt that: (1) Dico Consultants’ occupation and use of the Premises constituted a breach of the leasing instruments. (2) Apple Daily Printing, as the contracting party, was under a duty to disclose the breach to the Corporation under the leasing instruments. (3) Apple Daily Printing’s duty of disclosure was attributable to the applicants, so that their failure to disclose the breach to the Corporation constituted a concealment under section 16A. (4) Alternatively, the applicants were under an independent personal duty to disclose the breach to the Corporation. (5) Further or alternatively, the applicants made a false representation to the Corporation that the Premises had been used for the Specified Purpose.

criminal_law_hk.fraud.case_name: HKSAR v Mo Yuk Ping and Another
criminal_law_hk.fraud.proposition_text: The Court of Appeal held there is no general common-law duty to disclose one's own breach of contract, and a commercial lease did not create a special disclosure duty on these facts.
criminal_law_hk.fraud.supporting_quote: no general duty to disclose one’s own breach of contract
criminal_law_hk.fraud.exact_quote: no general duty to disclose one’s own breach of contract
criminal_law_hk.fraud.paragraph_text: 4. Applying well-established case law to the facts, the Court held that: (1) Dico Consultant’s occupation and use of the Premises constituted a breach of the leasing instruments. (2) In relation to concealment: (a) Under the common law, there is no general duty to disclose one’s own breach of contract. A lease does not generally fall within any established category of contracts where such a duty of disclosure is imposed. (b) In arguing that there was such a duty of disclosure imposed on Apple Daily Printing, the prosecution relied on express terms or alternatively implied terms of the leasing instruments; and the special nature of the instruments that gave rise to a special relationship between the parties. (c) However, the leasing instruments contained no such express term or, on a proper construction, such an implied term. (d) On the parties’ relationship, while the leasing instruments contained some special features, what existed between the parties was essentially a commercial landlord-tenant relationship: (i) As required by statute, the Corporation must act in accordance with prudent commercial principles. From its perspective, the relationship with the lessee was commercial in nature. So was the case from the lessee’s perspective. (ii) The preferential rates and tenure granted by the Corporation are important attractions to the lessee. However, the lessee has to satisfy the Corporation with the merits of its proposed projects in order to gain approval for admission to the Estate. One of the considerations taken into account by the Corporation was the size of investment proposed by the lessee. In the present case, Apple Daily Printing had invested HK$528 million into the construction of the Premises. Balancing the costs incurred and the benefits involved, including the preferential rates and tenure, to determine if the project was viable clearly entailed a careful commercial decision on Apple Daily Printing’s part. (iii) The Corporation’s decision to grant the lease to Apple Daily Printing was also a careful commercial decision ensuring that the grant of preferential rates and tenure was justified. (iv) Apple Daily Printing did not stand alone to benefit in terms of preferential rates and tenure. The Corporation would also benefit from the improvement in the land value from the construction of the Premises. Further, the Corporation must have been satisfied that Apple Daily Printing’s undertakings would facilitate the overall development of Hong Kong’s economy by broadening its industrial base and upgrading technology levels, which are substantial benefits that the Corporation, tasked by the Government to promote Hong Kong’s industry and technology, would stand to gain. (e) Accordingly, what existed between Apple Daily Printing and the Corporation was not a special relationship which constituted an exception to the common law rule that no duty of disclosure of breach arises in the performance of an already concluded contract. (f) Noting that the leasing instruments appeared to be standard contracts, the Court observed that if the prosecution were right on the duty of disclosure, it might potentially apply to all tenants in the Estate. The Court had reservations if such a sweeping proposition truly represented the Corporation’s leasing policy or contractual intent. (g) Even if Apple Daily Printing was under such a duty of disclosure, it could not as a matter of law be attributed to the applicants: (i) The prosecution did not rely on section 101E of the Criminal Procedure Ordinance, which is the most obvious route. (ii) The prosecution instead relied on the common law rule that corporate bodies are deemed to act and acquire knowledge through those individuals who are its directing mind. However, that rule attributes criminal liability to a company through the acts or omissions of its directing mind. It does not operate in an opposite way of attributing the company’s criminal liability to its officers. (h) The prosecution had not advanced any substantial submission why the applicants were under an independent personal duty of disclosure to the Corporation. (3) On the available evidence, the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the applicants had made the false representation that the Premises had been used for the Specified Purpose. (4) The Court therefore concluded that the prosecution had failed to prove the applicants had committed the actus reus of the fraud charges. (5) For completeness, in relation to mens rea , the Court observed that the trial judge had failed to consider certain important matters that were relevant to the applicants’ state of mind.

criminal_procedure_hk.invest_arrest_with.case_name: Secretary for Justice v Lam Tat Ming
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_arrest_with.proposition_text: A voluntary confession is prima facie admissible, but the court retains a residual discretion to exclude it to secure a fair trial.
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_arrest_with.supporting_quote: Where the court is so satisfied, the confession is admissible but the court retains a discretion to exclude it
criminal_procedure_hk.invest_arrest_with.paragraph_text: 1. In the criminal courts of Hong Kong, the prosecution in many cases relies as part of its case on confessions by the accused. Where the accused challenges the confession, the court usually holds a voir dire (i.e. a trial within a trial) to determine whether the prosecution has established that the confession was voluntary. Where the court is not so satisfied, the confession is inadmissible. Where the court is so satisfied, the confession is admissible but the court retains a discretion to exclude it. This has been called the residual discretion since it relates to evidence which is admissible.

criminal_procedure_hk.indictment_draftin.paragraph_text: 17. The exercise of the right of peaceful assembly, whether under the Basic Law or under BORO, may be subject to restrictions provided two requirements are satisfied : (1) The restriction must be prescribed by law (“the ‘prescribed by law’ requirement”). (2) The restriction must be necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security or public safety, public order (ordre public), the protection of public health or morals or the protection of the rights and freedoms of others (“the necessity requirement”).

criminal_procedure_hk.indictment_draftin.proposition_text: The necessity requirement imports a proportionality assessment for restrictions on fundamental rights.
